## The Shaft Is a Spring With a Memory {#sec-lay-ch15}

## A Concrete Picture

Bend a flexible ruler and release it. The ruler does not respond only to the
force you apply now. Its present shape and motion carry a short history of earlier
loading. It can return energy after your hand force has fallen, overshoot, and
vibrate in several patterns.

A golf shaft behaves far more subtly than the ruler, but the central point
survives: flexibility adds state. Treating the club as perfectly rigid may be
adequate for one question and misleading for another, especially when late
timing, grip moment, and impact-window energy are under study.

![A Prescribed Spring–Mass–Damper Motion Separates Stored Energy From Input Power and Damping Loss. This Is an Illustrative Energy Ledger, Not a Shaft Simulation.](figures/proximal_distal_companion/fig_companion_shaft_storage.svg){#fig-lay-shaft-storage width=96% fig-alt="Two panels show elastic and kinetic energy in joules, then signed drive power, damping loss and energy rate in watts during one prescribed displacement cycle."}

The illustration prescribes $x=A\sin^2(\pi t/T)$ with $A=0.025$ m,
$T=0.6$ s, $m=0.2$ kg, $k=80$ N/m and $c=0.8$ N s/m. The required drive
force is $m\ddot x+c\dot x+kx$, so input power minus $c\dot x^2$ equals
the rate of change of kinetic plus elastic energy. Negative drive power means
energy returns to the actuator; it does not label energy delivered to a clubhead.

## How the Mechanism Works

The simplest flexible model adds one coordinate $s$ for shaft deflection. Its
stored elastic energy might be $U_s=\tfrac12 k s^2$, and damping force might be
proportional to $\dot s$. The state now includes $s$ and $\dot s$. Grip work can
increase $U_s$; later shaft motion can return energy to rigid-body coordinates.

### Timing, Not Free Speed

An ideal passive spring stores and releases energy without creating it. Its
strain energy is not constant while it exchanges work with the rest of the
system. For a fixed linear stiffness $k>0$, $\dot U_s=ks\dot s$: the same
nonzero deformation can be storing or releasing energy. Mechanical energy is
conserved only for the complete conservative system with no net boundary work.
Damping converts mechanical energy to heat; contact can transfer energy to the
ball or other bodies.

The potentially useful feature is timing: accepting work and returning it when
the geometry and task make the transfer useful. That usefulness is an outcome
to test, not a property guaranteed by elasticity.

In a rigid-flexible comparison, the work-energy ledger must track boundary
input, gravity, damping and all retained kinetic and strain energy so that any
change in the specified delivery outcome has an accounted source.

### One Mode Versus a Distributed Shaft

A real shaft bends continuously. Modal analysis represents its shape as a sum of
vibration patterns. The first mode may capture most low-frequency deformation;
higher modes matter when excitation is rapid or spatially complex. A one-mode
model is efficient but should be compared with a higher-order beam reference.

An isolated structural study assembles an Euler–Bernoulli beam with tip mass and rotary
inertia, computes modal frequencies, identifies synthetic stiffness and mass,
and compares reduced responses. A separate study transports bending modes into
forward two-hand dynamics. Its baseline fails its declared small-deflection
screen, as discussed below; numerical closure does not remove that failure.
Mode truncation should be judged by specified load, power, energy and trajectory
errors, not by appearance or frequency agreement alone.

### Excitation Decides Required Complexity

Slow loading may barely excite high modes, making a rigid or one-mode model
adequate. A sharp command, impact, or rapid contact change can excite them. The
right model therefore depends on the frequency content of the question.

This is analogous to describing ocean swell with one broad wave versus describing
a splash. More modes are not inherently more truthful; they are needed when the
input and observable are sensitive to them.

### Interface Power Connects Hand and Shaft

For an ideal point load $F$ at a deforming shaft station, write its material-point
velocity as $v=V+\omega\times r+B\dot\eta$. Here $V$ and $\omega$ describe
the reference motion, $r$ is the current offset, and $B\dot\eta$ is the relative
deformation velocity. In one observer frame the same power can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
P&=F\cdot v\\
 &=F\cdot V+(r\times F)\cdot\omega\\
 &\quad +(B^TF)\cdot\dot\eta.
\end{aligned}
$$

These are two representations of one port. Adding the last modal term to
$F\cdot v$ would count deformation power twice. Applied contact moments require
their own compatible angular-velocity decomposition. A resultant wrench alone
represents all contact power only when the interface motion is rigid, or the
unrepresented deformation power vanishes. Distributed tractions can do work on
deformation even when their net wrench is zero.

The flexible model separates grip moment from internal shaft moment. A negative
grip couple can coexist with shaft energy release and positive club kinetic-
energy growth. This makes the shaft relevant to the negative-torque discussion
without turning it into the sole explanation.

### Impact Is a Severe Boundary

Near ball contact, high-frequency response and contact duration matter. A model
that stops at a pre-impact criterion can discuss delivery but not claim a full
impact prediction. A distributed shaft needs measured stiffness, damping,
geometry, clubhead inertia, grip conditions, and timestep resolution before it
becomes equipment calibration.

**Model Result:** The isolated beam and articulated first-mode atlas report
bounded synthetic checks. The separate planar forward-modal baseline retains
numerical coupling evidence but fails its small-deflection screen. These are
different models and acceptance results, not interchangeable validation claims.

**Human Evidence:** Betzler and colleagues tested 20 golfers with two clubs
designed to differ in shaft bending stiffness. The less stiff club produced a
small average clubhead-speed increase, alongside changes in shaft recovery and
grip motion; the authors judged the overall effects small for the shafts tested
[@betzler2012]. This does not identify a universal fitting rule or calibrate the
synthetic models here. Strain or optical measurements need their own calibration
and uncertainty treatment.

**Hypothesis:** Shaft state may mediate how a late negative grip couple and
proximal power coexist, returning stored energy while the grip channel opposes
rotation.

**Practical Interpretation:** Flex behaves like short-term mechanical memory:
what the shaft does now depends on how it was loaded and how fast that loading
changed.

### What the Shaft Adds to the State

A rigid club needs pose, including orientation, and compatible linear and angular
velocity. A flexible shaft needs
additional deformation coordinates and their rates. A one-mode model might use
one bending amplitude; a distributed beam uses many modes or elements. These
states carry memory because current shaft force depends not only on grip and
clubhead position but also on how the shaft is bent and moving.

That memory complicates matched-state comparisons. Two swings with identical
grip and clubhead pose can have different shaft curvature or modal velocity.
Removing a command from those apparently identical frames can produce different
responses. Within the same flexible model, a same-state intervention must match
the complete state, including activation or contact-memory variables if present.
Between rigid and flexible models, the state spaces differ: declare a mapping
of common pose and velocity, the elastic initial state, mass properties, contact
geometry and energy. Equal rigid coordinates alone do not establish equal total
energy or a compatible constrained state.

### Loading, Storage, and Return

When relative motion bends or twists the shaft, load power can increase strain
energy. Inertial coupling redistributes energy; it is not a separate external
energy supply. Damping turns some mechanical energy into
heat. As deformation changes, the shaft can return energy to the rigid motion
of grip and head. Return is not guaranteed to occur in the useful direction or
at the useful time; phase matters.

It is tempting to say the shaft “kicks” the clubhead. A better account plots
strain energy, damping loss, power at grip and head interfaces, and modal phase.
If shaft energy decreases while clubhead kinetic energy increases, return may be
part of the explanation, but whole-system closure and other power ports still
matter.

### A Simple Spring Thought Experiment

Take a spring with stiffness $k$ and displacement $x$. Stored energy is
$\tfrac12kx^2$. Doubling deformation quadruples energy, but a real shaft's
distributed bending and torsion do not reduce exactly to one scalar spring. Add
damping and a changing boundary, and release timing depends on natural
frequencies, mode shapes, and excitation history.

If the downswing duration aligns poorly with a mode, extra bending can return
too late or increase presentation variability. A linear spring in static
equilibrium stores $F^2/(2k)$ under a prescribed force, so increasing $k$ reduces
storage in that comparison. At fixed displacement it stores $kx^2/2$, so
increasing $k$ increases storage instead. Dynamic loading also depends on inertia,
damping and drive frequency: resonance can reverse a simple stiffness trend.
Increasing stiffness raises $\sqrt{k/m}$ only with the same effective mass and
boundary model; it does not guarantee a faster useful response. There is no
universal “more flex equals more speed” rule.

### Interaction With the Negative-Couple Mechanism

A two-hand couple loads the handle and can excite shaft bending or torsion.
Shaft reaction then changes the wrench at the hands and the clubhead's future
state. A negative contact couple may partly regulate deformation, or it may be a
reaction to deformation generated elsewhere. Causal separation requires
killswitches and energy accounting in the flexible model.

Compare rigid, one-mode, and distributed-shaft rungs with an explicit initial-
state mapping and the same endpoint definition. Does the late couple retain
sign? Does its timing shift with modal
frequency? Does a speed benefit remain after shaft strain energy and damping are
accounted for? If a mechanism vanishes in the flexible rung, that is important
evidence about the rigid approximation.

### Interaction With Preload and Slack

Continuous hand loading can maintain shaft deformation through transition,
while a role reversal can unload and reload one mode. Yet “shaft preload” is not
the same as muscle or grip preload. The shaft may remain bent while a hand-force
component crosses zero, or vice versa. Each state requires its own measurement.

The phenomenological dead zone should not absorb shaft dynamics implicitly. If
shaft deformation is modeled, transmission parameters and modal states must be
identifiable enough to avoid two mechanisms explaining the same delay. Ablation
tests—rigid shaft, zero dead zone, altered damping—show which declared model
mechanism changes the result. They do not by themselves identify the mechanism
in a golfer; distinct models can still fit the same observations.

### Model Validation Ladder

Begin with static deflection under known loads. Continue with free-vibration
frequency and damping tests, then dynamic boundary excitation. Verify modal
convergence and timestep stability. Compare strain, tip displacement, and
energy balance with an independent beam or finite-element reference. These are
verification steps. After coupling to the swing, repeat the power, convergence
and deformation-domain checks: a sound isolated beam can be driven outside its
valid range by the coupled model. Experimental validation is a separate step.

Human validation uses instrumented clubs with calibrated strain or optical
shape measures. Club properties should be measured, not selected merely from a
label such as “stiff.” Repeated trials reveal whether deformation phase and
contact wrench are consistent within a golfer. Equipment changes should be
bounded and randomized to reduce learning and expectation effects.

### What a Shaft Result Can Support

A validated model can say that, under declared properties and motion, certain
modal forces, powers, and energy exchanges occurred. It can predict how a
controlled property change shifts them. It cannot infer a golfer's preferred
feel, injury risk, or universal fitting recommendation without additional data.

For the proximal-distal framework, the shaft is most valuable as a test of
mechanism survival. If the interaction and allocation conclusions remain under
realistic flexibility and uncertainty, confidence grows. If not, the model
ladder has found the boundary where the simpler explanation must be revised.

### Reader Lab: Watch Phase Change the Answer

Excite a declared one-mode shaft model with the same peak handle force at three
different times. Plot deformation, modal velocity, strain energy, grip power,
head power, and damping loss. The same force magnitude can store or return
different energy because phase and boundary motion differ. Equal peaks do not
match force history, impulse or work; report those differences too.

Copy two states with identical rigid pose and velocity but opposite modal
velocity. Apply the same future hand wrench and test whether the chosen
clubhead observable differs. Symmetry, mode coupling or observation timing can
hide a state difference; a different internal state does not guarantee a
different measured endpoint.

Next, reset shaft deformation and modal velocity to zero while retaining the
rigid coordinates and rates. This is a model intervention with a new initial
condition. Record its energy change, momentum change and any constraint or
contact projection. Removing strain energy does not necessarily reduce total
energy: rigid–modal cross terms in kinetic energy can change either way. The
reset requires explicit work and impulse bookkeeping before interpreting the
subsequent trajectory. It is not an available human command or a measured
causal contribution in a golfer.

Repeat the negative-couple branch across stiffness and damping. Report whether
couple sign, onset, work, and terminal speed remain. A result that survives
realistic property uncertainty deserves more confidence than one tuned to a
single resonance.

### Avoiding Double Explanations

If both a dead-zone transmission and flexible shaft can produce delay, fit or
vary them jointly. Look for observables that separate them: grip force may change
before shaft strain under one mechanism, while modal phase dominates another.
Without such information, their parameters can compensate and neither is
identifiable.

The release should therefore include ablations and joint sensitivity, not one
best-fit flexible trace. When two explanations remain equivalent, the honest
output is an experiment recommendation—usually synchronized wrench and shaft
state—rather than a preferred story.

### A Minimum Flexible-Club Result

At minimum, publish the measured or declared club properties, modal frequencies
and damping, deformation and modal velocity, grip and head power, strain-energy
history, damping loss, and work-energy residual. Show timestep and modal
convergence. Declare the rigid-to-flexible state mapping and distinguish fixed-
input comparisons from comparisons selected to match an outcome.

Then qualify the conclusion. A synthetic property sweep shows mechanical
possibility and sensitivity. A calibrated participant club permits predictions
for that equipment; held-out observations test their accuracy. Replication can
extend support only across the equipment, golfers and conditions actually tested.
Skipping these levels turns shaft “memory” into a metaphor too broad to fail.

### The Registered Test Says the Benefit Is Not Universal

The [articulated shaft atlas](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/a1a613999eb0c744da96caa040941955eb210a21/docs/research/proximal_distal_energy_transfer/data/articulated_shaft_atlas.json)
tests a passive synthetic shaft with the first bending shape in each of two
orthogonal planes, plus torsion. These are not the first and second bending
frequencies in one plane. Bending is anchored to a 24-element reference at
5.2399 Hz; torsion is declared at 70.1260 Hz. Twelve initial states, four
activations (rigid, bending, torsion, coupled), two velocity branches, two
timesteps and two engines give **384 trajectories**. The motion starts from
initial conditions, with no active driver or joint torque. Zero modal coordinates
and rates give a common initial energy in this declared comparison. The velocity
branches add $\pm0.05$ m/s to club-frame $x$ translation; the timesteps are
0.25 and 0.125 ms, using MuJoCo and Pinocchio. Five tension-only spring–damper
stations per hand supply grip loads and grip dissipation. These are synthetic
contact elements, not measured fingers or pressure distributions.

The observed maxima are 1.696 mm of tip bend and 0.00186 rad of twist; these are
results, not the acceptance thresholds. The configured limits are 5% of the
1.08 m shaft length (54 mm) and 10 degrees of twist (about 0.175 rad). Two
additional coarse-timestep probes that left the linear domain were excluded and
reported separately; they do not reduce the accepted 384-trajectory grid.

The coupled-versus-rigid comparison uses four horizons: 4, 10, 25 and 50 ms.
Its **384 comparison cells** count twelve states, two velocity branches, two
timesteps, two engines and four horizons. This happens to equal the trajectory
count, but counts something different. Repeated horizons, engines and timesteps
are not independent golfer trials.

Only **126 of 384** comparison cells pass the post-registration load-and-work
matching rule: 28 at 4 ms, zero at 10 ms, 40 at 25 ms and 58 at 50 ms. For each
quantity $a,b$, the rule is

$$
\frac{|a-b|}{\max\{f,(|a|+|b|)/2\}}\leq0.05.
$$

The floor $f$ is 1 N for the largest station-force norm over the horizon and
$10^{-6}$ J for grip-plus-shaft damping loss. When the mean magnitude falls
below its floor, the absolute tolerances are 0.05 N and $5\times10^{-8}$ J,
respectively. These compare dissipation, not total grip boundary work.
Selecting cells by these two outcomes is a descriptive
comparison; it does not match every load history or identify a causal shaft
effect in a golfer.

Across those selected cells, the reported coupled-minus-rigid speed difference is
**$-0.0285$ to $+0.0212$ m/s**. Both signs appear. Crucially, the
[recording code](https://github.com/D-sorganization/UpstreamDrift/blob/a1a613999eb0c744da96caa040941955eb210a21/scripts/research/proximal_distal_energy/articulated_shaft_atlas.py)
uses the norm of the club-frame translation rates, with origin at the modeled
grip mass. This omits the rotational
and deformation contributions to clubhead-point velocity. It is measured at
fixed horizons, not at impact. Sometimes the flexible shaft is slower **in this
translation-speed observable**; the quoted interval is not an impact clubhead-
speed interval. At 50 ms alone, the matched range is $-0.0208$ to $+0.00634$ m/s.

A positive effect on this observable is therefore **rejected as a universal
rule** within the registered synthetic comparison. A human clubhead-speed or
equipment-fitting conclusion requires a different endpoint and calibrated data.
The atlas also omits ground reaction and free moment, so it cannot establish a
contribution from the feet.

Two other studies answer different questions. In the isolated beam reference,
one-mode versus six-mode tip-displacement RMS disagreement rises from about
$0.69$ micrometres under an 80 ms pulse to $41$ micrometres under a 4 ms pulse
with a different force-and-moment input. That comparison motivates checking
excitation and truncation; it is not a universal frequency cutoff. In the
separate planar forward-modal baseline, maximum absolute modal tip displacement
is **13.48% of shaft length**, above its **5%** screen. Its small contact-power
residual verifies a coupling identity but cannot establish valid small-
deflection dynamics outside the screen. The articulated atlas passing its own
checks does not repair this distinct baseline.

### Chapter Checkpoint

Before crediting shaft return, check the complete state, energy-transfer
direction, damping and ledger closure. Test the specified endpoint across
property uncertainty and independent models. Distinguish verification, domain
screens and held-out validation. The current translation-speed result supports
both signs of change; clubhead-speed and individual control/load tradeoffs still
require calibrated human data.

## Where the Picture Breaks

The ruler bends in one obvious plane. Shafts bend and twist in space, taper, vary
in material, and interact with a distributed grip and clubhead. Classical
Euler–Bernoulli bending neglects shear deformation and distributed beam rotary
inertia; a tip body's rotary inertia can still be included, as in this reference.
Torsion requires its own model. Synthetic parameter recovery checks an inverse
pipeline under its generating assumptions, not equipment validity.

The phrase “kick” can also imply a free late boost. Any returned energy was
previously supplied and survived damping. A fair comparison counts the complete
cycle.
